card.title: Notice Writing + Formal & Informal Writing Mastery

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Notices are 50-word impersonal announcements with five locked components; formal and informal writing differ across contractions, vocabulary, sentence length and person; and every format is the same purpose-driven skeleton in different clothes. Master the skeleton, the register switches and the paragraph architecture, and any writing prompt becomes executable.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
NOTICE = body name + NOTICE + date + heading + body(what/when/where/who) + name + designation; ≤50 words; no salutation.
FORMAL LETTER = address → date → receiver → subject → salutation → why → details → action → faithfully + full name.
INFORMAL LETTER = address → date → Dear Name → ack → news → warm close → With love + first name.

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: ❌ Writing 'Dear Sir' in a notice. ✅ Notices have no salutation — they are impersonal announcements.  ·  ❌ Signing a notice with a first name only. ✅ Full name + designation + issuing body.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: In the exam, write the format skeleton first — format marks are the cheapest marks available.  ·  Keep a personal register-switch table of 10 formal↔informal pairs; revise before every exam.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Specimen notice: NOTICE / 15 March 2026 / INTER-HOUSE DEBATE / An inter-house debate will be held on 22 March 2026 at 10 a.m. in the school hall. Two participants per house. — Anita Rai, Secretary, Literary Club  ·  Same news, two registers: Formal — 'The Literary Club cordially invites...' / Informal — 'Hey! The debate is finally happening...'

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: ❌ 'Yours sincerely' after 'Dear Sir/Madam'. ✅ Unnamed → faithfully; named → sincerely.  ·  ❌ Contractions in formal writing. ✅ 'cannot', 'will not' — contractions mark informality.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: **What this covers:** the complete mechanics of notices (the shortest high-mark format) and the full contrast between formal and informal writing — so that after reading, you can produce ANY piece of English writing with the right register, structure and tone.  ·  **NOTICE — the 5 locked components in order:** 1) the word NOTICE (top-centre, or the issuing body's name above it) 2) DATE of issue 3) HEADING (what the notice is about, centred, bold) 4) BODY (answers What/When/Where/Who in 3-4 sentences, max ~50 words) 5) SIGNATURE block (name, designation, issuing body — bottom-left).

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Count words for the notice FIRST — then write to fit.  ·  Letter to the editor: para 3 usually asks authorities to act.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Q1. Notice as Head Girl: blood-donation camp (≤50 words).  ·  Q2. Formal letter to the Principal requesting extra library hours during exams.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: This page + the Grammar Master Mindmap + Grammar Hacks = complete coverage of English writing and grammar.

rows.label: Classified table
rows.text: Notice vs letter vs essay — classified by purpose and shape · Feature | Notice | Formal letter | Essay · Purpose | Announce to many | Request one reader | Argue a position · Length | 50 words or fewer | Medium, structured | Long, developed · Frame | Box heading NOTICE + date + signature | Addresses + salutation + closing | Intro-body-conclusion · Voice | Third person, no pleasantries | Courteous, exact | Argumentative, flowing

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Notices: 5 components, ≤50 words, third person, future tense for events.  ·  Faithfully (unnamed) vs Sincerely (named) — an automatic mark.  ·  Formal = no contractions, objective; Informal = contractions, warmth.  ·  Every paragraph: topic → support → link.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: All English prose formats share one skeleton: opening (purpose) → middle (detail) → closing (action/feeling).  ·  Register is signalled by four levers: contractions, vocabulary, sentence length, person.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: Q3. Informal letter to a friend describing how you spent Dashain.  ·  Q4. Convert to informal: 'Please accept my sincere apologies for the inconvenience caused.'

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: Paragraph dissected: topic ('Morning walks transform health') → supports (air, routine, sunlight) → link ('The mind benefits just as much...')

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **NOTICE — the 50-word law:** examiners deduct for length. Every word must carry information: 'The school is organising...' ❌ → 'An inter-house debate will be held...' ✅  ·  **NOTICE — no personal touches:** no 'Dear students', no first/second person. Passive voice and third person only: 'Students are informed that...'. Signature = name + designation only.  ·  **NOTICE — tense logic:** upcoming events → future (will be held); results → present perfect (has been selected).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: PARAGRAPH = Topic + 2-3 Support + Link; ONE idea per paragraph.  ·  Register levers: no contractions + Latinate vocab + long sentences + 3rd person = formal.  ·  Tense by format: report=past, notice=future, essay=present, story=past.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ A 90-word notice. ✅ Stay ~50 words; extra sentences risk deduction.  ·  A notice never addresses the reader directly — it informs in the third person.  ·  One paragraph = one idea, developed with support and closed with a link.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Formal writing persuades with structure; informal writing connects with warmth.  ·  Story stuck? Setting → problem → twist → resolution.  ·  Subject line: topic + purpose in one line.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Draft a notice (≤50 words): Eco Club tree-plantation drive next Saturday; register by Thursday.  ·  Write the opening and closing paragraphs of a letter to the editor about reckless honking near a school.  ·  Rewrite informally: 'I regret to inform you that I shall be unable to attend.' ('So sorry — I can't make it.')

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Identify the format: past tense, passive voice, heading, findings — (report.)  ·  Build one paragraph on 'morning walks': topic sentence + two supports + link.  ·  Examiners grade structure first (format components), then language, then content.
